title: The four-day week experiment
text:
What would you do with an extra day off every week? For the employees of more than sixty British companies, this was not just a dream. In 2022, they took part in one of the largest trials of a four-day working week ever carried out. They worked eighty percent of their usual hours, but kept one hundred percent of their pay – on the condition that they remained just as productive.

The results surprised many sceptics. At the end of the six-month trial, the vast majority of the companies decided to continue with the new system, and only a handful returned to the traditional five-day week. Revenue stayed roughly the same, and in some firms it even rose slightly. At the same time, the number of sick days fell, and fewer employees left their jobs.

"People simply waste less time when they know the week is shorter," explains Dr Helen Marsh, a researcher who analysed the data. "Meetings become shorter, and unnecessary tasks disappear. Employees think much more carefully about what really matters."

The employees themselves reported lower levels of stress and better sleep. Many said that the extra day allowed them to deal with personal matters, such as doctor's appointments or shopping, so that the weekend could finally be used for rest. Parents in particular appreciated having more time with their children.

However, the four-day week is not a solution for everyone. Critics point out that most of the companies in the trial were small and worked in offices, where output is relatively easy to organise. In hospitals, schools or factories, things are much more complicated. "You cannot ask a nurse to look after the same number of patients in four days instead of five," says economist Mark Doyle. "Someone else has to do the work on the fifth day, and that costs money."

Another problem is that some employees found the shorter week more intense. With less time to complete the same tasks, a few of them felt more pressure, not less. Some managers also admitted that it was difficult to arrange meetings when each team member had a different day off.

Despite these concerns, interest in the idea is growing. Several countries, including Spain, Portugal and Iceland, have run their own trials, and many technology companies now offer a shorter week to attract the best candidates. Whether it will ever become the norm remains to be seen. For now, it seems that for the right kind of company, working less really can mean working better.
